opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by "work." For a huge share of knowledge work, like writing code, analyzing documents, or answering questions, you can get remarkably far with language alone. We've seen that very clearly in the last few years. Those tasks are already digitized and symbolic, and you can often verify the result without ever predicting what the world will look like next.

Where vision world models become really necessary is when an AI has to act in the physical world. Robotics is the obvious case. If a robot is folding laundry, cooking, or working in a warehouse or a home, it needs to anticipate what will happen if it pushes this object or grasps it from that angle. Will it slip? Will the stack fall over? You can't easily capture all of that in words, because so much of it is continuous, spatial, and governed by physics. It's also expensive and sometimes dangerous to learn everything by trial and error in the real world, so being able to imagine outcomes before acting is hugely valuable. Autonomous driving is similar: you need to predict how the scene will evolve and how other agents will behave, and the cost of mistakes is very high.

There's also a middle ground that I find interesting, which is digital work that's inherently visual. Think about an agent using a computer interface, or doing design, video, or scientific imaging. There you certainly need strong vision, but you may not need a full world model in the sense of predicting future frames in detail. Often, a model just has to predict the parts that matter for the task, and I think that's an important point. A world model doesn't necessarily need to reconstruct every pixel. The tree moving in the background usually doesn't matter if your goal is to pick up a cup.

So my short answer is that if the work lives in the digital, symbolic world, vision world models may be helpful but often aren't essential. Once the work involves physical interaction, where actions have consequences that you have to anticipate, I think they become very hard to avoid. That's also why I think we're still relatively early. We have very capable language models, but physical intelligence still has a long way to go, and better world models could be one of the key pieces to bridge that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says language alone can handle much digital knowledge work and that vision world models are often not essential for work in the digital, symbolic world.

r002.rationale: It mentions agents using computer interfaces but does not say that direct screen access avoids manually supplying screenshots.

r003.rationale: It ties physical work to anticipating action outcomes and to continuous spatial physics, but does not identify fine-grained visual feedback as the reason vision world models are needed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is: it depends a lot on what you mean by "work," and I try to separate the cases where you genuinely need a model of how the visual world evolves from the cases where people say "world model" but really just mean good perception.

Let me start with where I think they're clearly necessary. Anything embodied. If you want a robot to pick up a mug, fold laundry, or navigate a kitchen it hasn't seen before, the system has to have some prediction of what happens after it acts. Not just "this is a mug" but "if I push here, it tips, and the handle rotates toward me." That's a dynamics problem, and vision is the primary sensor. You can get surprisingly far with imitation and a strong policy network, but the moment you need to plan over several steps, or recover from a mistake, you need something that can simulate forward. The same goes for autonomous driving. The hard cases aren't recognition, they're anticipation: that pedestrian is going to step off the curb, that car is about to merge.

The second category is anything where the model has to act in a visual interface over time. Computer-use agents are the obvious example. People sometimes think a screenshot plus a strong language model is enough, and for short tasks it often is. But longer tasks require the agent to understand that clicking this button opens a modal, that scrolling changes what's visible, that the state has changed even though nothing told you explicitly. That's a world model, even if it's a very mundane world.

Now the part I'd push back on a little. For a lot of what we currently call "AI doing work," which is mostly text, code, and analysis, I don't think a vision world model is necessary at all. And even in vision, a lot of tasks are fundamentally static. Medical image reading, document understanding, inspecting a product on a manufacturing line. Those need strong representations, and we've learned a lot about how to get those from large-scale pretraining, but they don't need the model to predict the next frame.

The thing I'm actually most interested in is the middle. There's a question of whether predicting the future of a video is the right objective to get good representations in the first place. The intuition from language is that next-token prediction gives you everything. In vision, I'm less sure. Pixel-level prediction spends a lot of capacity on things that don't matter, like exactly how leaves move in the wind. So I think the open question isn't just "where are world models necessary," it's "at what level of abstraction should the world model live." Predicting in a learned latent space, or predicting the consequences of actions rather than the appearance of the scene, seems more promising to me than raw video generation, even though the video generation results are the ones that look impressive.

So short version: necessary for embodied agents and for anything interactive over time; not necessary for most perception tasks; and the interesting research question is what the right representation for a world model actually is.

r001.rationale: The response says most current AI work—text, code, and analysis—does not require a vision world model.

r002.rationale: It discusses computer-use agents and screenshots, but does not identify direct access to the user's screen as a way to avoid manually supplying screenshots.

r003.rationale: It links physical tasks to predicting action consequences and planning, but does not attribute the need specifically to fine-grained visual feedback.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re particularly useful when an AI system needs to act in the physical world. In robotics, for example, recognizing what’s in an image is only part of the problem. The robot also needs to anticipate what will happen if it takes an action. If I push this object, where will it move? If I pick it up, what happens to the objects around it? A world model could help the system predict those consequences before acting.

But I wouldn’t say every task requires a vision world model. For many tasks, understanding the current image and producing an answer may be enough. The stronger case is when you need to plan over multiple steps, when actions change the environment, and when trying things in the real world is expensive or risky.

And there’s a distinction between generating a realistic-looking video and having a model that’s useful for doing work. For planning, the important thing is whether the predictions capture the consequences of your actions reliably enough to help you make better decisions.

I think they’re especially useful when an AI system needs to act in the physical world. For a robot, recognizing what’s in an image is only part of the problem. It also needs to understand what might happen if it takes an action—if it pushes an object, for example, where will that object go? A world model could let it predict those outcomes and plan before actually doing something.

But I wouldn’t say every task requires a vision world model. For many recognition tasks, or work that happens entirely through text, you may not need one. The stronger case is where the system has to reason about how a visual environment changes over time and how its actions affect that environment. And even there, the question is how much of the world you need to model. You probably don’t need to predict every pixel perfectly; you need to capture the things that matter for the task.
